title: Nanospike attenuation run notes
content:
Goal:
Quick investigation into tiny, high-frequency request spikes ("nanospikes") that cause transient p99+/p999 latency blips without sustained QPS increase. Hypothesis: short bursts interact with batching window + GPU kernel warmup creating amplification events.

Environment:
- Model: llama-3-medium-v1 (fp16), 8k context, kv-cache enabled
- Serving variant: quantized int8-fastpath (experiment branch)
- Hardware: single A100-40GB (dedicated pool simulation)
- Runtime: rwl-2.3.1+local-patch (batching window tunables exposed)
- Workload generator: custom Go harness (sync vs async modes), ~5ms client-side jitter

Config for baseline run (R0):
- target QPS: 120 steady
- arrival pattern: Poisson with intermittent 30-40 req/s nanospikes for 200ms every 10s
- max_batch_tokens: 4096
- batch_timeout_ms: 8
- concurrency_per_worker: 12
- kv_cache_hit_rate: ~0.76 (synthetic warm prefix)

Commands used:
- ./bench --qps=120 --pattern=nanospike --spike_rate=35 --spike_dur_ms=200 --period_ms=10000 --clients=24
- curl -sS -X POST http://localhost:8080/debug/metrics | grep "batch_window"

Observed metrics (R0) - aggregated 5m window:
- throughput (tokens/s): 18200
- p50 latency (ms): 22
- p95 latency (ms): 68
- p99 latency (ms): 182
- p999 latency (ms): 642
- GPU util: 45-58% (spiky)
- batch size (mean): 6 tokens per request equivalence; mean requests per batch: 11

Inline timeline snapshot (ASCII sparkline of p99 over 2 min; each char ~2s):
..__..^^..__..^^..__..^^..__..^^..
Legend: '.' idle-ish, '_' normal elevation, '^' nanospike-induced blip

Quick reproduction of severe blip (R1) - tweak: batch_timeout_ms -> 16ms
- p99 -> 310ms, p999 -> 1200ms (worse)
- root cause clue: longer batch windows coalesce more requests during nanospike leading to bigger kernel occupancy spikes and scheduling backpressure.

Alternate tweak (R2): batch_timeout_ms -> 4ms, concurrency_per_worker -> 18, preemptive_flush=true
- p99 -> 96ms, p999 -> 420ms (improved for spikes)
- tradeoffs: average tokens/s down ~6% (more small batches), GPU utilization more stable (42-49%)

Micro-observations from profiler traces:
- 1) During 200ms nanospike, queue depth jumps ~3.7x; runtime schedules a large concat-batch op that lasts ~120ms on GPU (kernel warmup + larger memory ops)
- 2) KV cache misses slightly increase during spike windows (our synthetic prefixes misalign) causing a small extra 8-12ms per request per miss
- 3) When batch_timeout higher, batches include a small number of very short-context requests and some long-context ones -> variance in token decode steps; tail amplifies

Hypotheses / interpretations:
- Nanospikes produce a mismatch between batching policy (aiming to increase throughput) and per-request time variance that collectively causes tail amplification via two mechanisms: large GPU kernel occupies the device longer; and scheduler backlog increases queuing latency for new requests -> p999 balloon.
- Longer batch windows increase throughput but make the system less robust to short spikes. Preemptive flush and tighter timeouts reduce tail but cost throughput.

Quick actionables (experimental):
1) Implement adaptive batch timeout: if ingress rate derivative > threshold -> reduce batch_timeout to 3-4ms for 300ms window. (Experiment ID: NS-2026-A)
2) Try request-size aware batching to avoid mixing very short vs long requests in same batch. (NS-2026-B)
3) Add a lightweight kernel-shed metric to routing: if a single batch kernel > 80ms, throttle new batch formation for 100ms to let device drain. (NS-2026-C)
4) Re-run with a better kv-cache priming so spike prefixes don't bias misses (control run).

Planned next runs and matrix:
- R3: adaptive_timeout=true, derivative_thresh=10rps/s, measurement 10m
- R4: request-size-aware=true, threshold=token_count_var>2x
- R5: simulate real client jitter (10-40ms) + nanospike to check interplay

Notes to self:
- Capture full perf traces (trace IDs) for top 3 p999 examples; link to PR for adaptive_timeout skeleton.
- Talk to Marta about adding small ‘fastpath’ kernel variant for batches <8 reqs.

References / quick links:
- Git PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2345
- Jira: SERV-7892 (nanospike tail investigation)
- Slack thread: slack:/archives/C01234567/p1678901234567

TL;DR:
Short spikes (200ms) can produce outsized p999 latency via batching-policy interaction and kernel occupancy. Shorter timeouts and preemptive flush reduce tails at the cost of modest throughput loss. Next: try adaptive_timeout heuristic+request-size-aware batching to aim for best-of-both.
